endorsements.quote: In general, we recommend that the use of LLM-based consent should not change accountability standards for research.
Finally, it will likely be necessary to introduce LLMs into CRC in a staged approach, to allow time for both researchers and participants to adapt to a new system.
Secondly, LLM interactions should be monitored by human-in-the-loop processes to ensure accuracy and accountability.
Public engagement forums and mechanisms for participant feedback are essential to ensure trust in these systems, alongside stringent adherence to data privacy and security standards.
Institutions should also be transparent about how participants’ data is used and stored.

It would therefore be essential that LLMs are programmed to recognise the limits of their capabilities, and to refer users to human researchers when questions exceed the AI’s scope of knowledge or when a human-based approach is required.
For example, the LLM could be programmed with fact-checking mechanisms using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ( Lewis et al., 2020 ).
Initial introduction of LLM-based consent processes should also allow participants to have the option to follow up with a researcher after an LLM interaction if they so choose.

unlisted_practices: Deploy institutional LLMs for research consent within closed networks to protect participants' data privacy and security.
Have IRBs pre-approve LLM base consent scripts and training data and audit a random sample of consent transcripts and interaction reports.
Program LLMs to generate consent interaction reports flagging participant confusion or hesitancy for researcher review.
Offer participants a choice between traditional consent, LLM-based consent, or both.
Ensure LLM-based consent is no more or less persuasive than human consent processes.
Reform regulations to permit more flexible consent language if LLMs replace written participant information sheets.
Embed the LLM within a consent platform with fixed parameters ensuring all key study information is mentioned at least once.
Establish a real-time human intervention process and contingency plan for LLM errors in consent.
Consider no-fault compensation for participants harmed by LLM errors in the consent process.

screen.reason: This is an ethical commentary and policy framework exploring the implications of using LLMs for informed consent in clinical research, proposing implementation models and recommendations for researchers and IRBs.
